explanations.explanation: That's him, friend. The LORD tells Moses to cross the Arnon Valley and says, “See, I have delivered into your hand Sihon the Amorite, king of Heshbon, and his land.” Sihon is the first king Moses names in this retelling. Og, king of Bashan, comes later in the passage.

Balak was king of Moab (Numbers 22:4), but he isn't in this passage. Moab did come up earlier, as a land Israel was told not to harass (Deuteronomy 2:9), so I see why it was on your mind. The king here is Sihon the Amorite, king of Heshbon. Easy to grab the cutter next to the one you wanted, friend. I've done it plenty.

Hiram was king of Tyre (1 Kings 5:1), but he doesn't show up anywhere in these verses. The LORD names Sihon the Amorite, king of Heshbon, and says He has delivered Sihon and his land into Israel's hand. Kings do tend to blur together, like two batches that came out of the oven looking identical.

This one flips it around, friend. With Moab, Israel was told not to harass them or provoke them to war (Deuteronomy 2:9). With Sihon, the LORD says, “Begin to take possession of it and engage him in battle.” So the instruction this time is the opposite of leaving the land alone.

Right, it's False. The LORD tells Israel, “Begin to take possession of it and engage him in battle.” That's a very different instruction from the ones about Esau's descendants (Deuteronomy 2:4-5) and Moab (Deuteronomy 2:9), where Israel was told not to provoke them. Same road, different orders.

The LORD says, “They will hear the reports of you and tremble in anguish because of you.” Hearing the reports is enough to shake them. You know when a boss's reputation walks into the room before he does, and everybody is already sitting up straight? That's the idea. And notice the LORD says this very day He begins to put that dread and fear on them.

explanations.answer: They will send gifts of peace
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. The LORD doesn't mention gifts at all. He says He will put dread and fear of Israel on the nations, and that they will “…tremble in anguish…” There's no welcome party in this verse.

explanations.answer: They will gather to fight back
explanations.explanation: That's not what the LORD says here. He says the nations will hear the reports and “…tremble in anguish…” The word is dread and fear, not a battle plan. The verse stays on how they feel when the news reaches them.

Yes, friend. Moses says, “So from the Wilderness of Kedemoth I sent messengers with an offer of peace to Sihon king of Heshbon…” The LORD had already told Israel to engage Sihon in battle (Deuteronomy 2:24), and still the messengers go out with an offer of peace. They show up with an open hand.
Close in spirit, maybe, but that's not what Moses says. The messengers carry “…an offer of peace…” Nothing in the verse tells Sihon to give up anything. They are asking to pass through.

Not this time, friend. Moses sends messengers “…with an offer of peace…” The war part comes later in the passage, and it begins when Sihon comes out to fight. The first thing in the messengers' hands is peace.

explanations.answer: To pay for it in silver
explanations.explanation: That's it. Moses says, “You can sell us food to eat and water to drink in exchange for silver.” They aren't asking for a handout, they're asking to be customers. Everybody likes the customer who shows up with exact change.

explanations.answer: To bring their own from Moab
explanations.explanation: Moses doesn't say that, friend. He offers that Sihon can sell them food and water, “…in exchange for silver.” Moab only comes up in the verses next to this one, as one of the places that let Israel pass. The plan here is to buy from Sihon.

explanations.answer: To ask for it as a gift
explanations.explanation: Moses is offering the opposite. He says, “You can sell us food to eat and water to drink in exchange for silver.” They plan to pay. A gift isn't part of the offer.

Right, it's True. Moses says Israel is asking to pass through “…just as the descendants of Esau who live in Seir and the Moabites who live in Ar did for us…” He's pointing to others who already said yes. It's like telling a shop owner, "Everybody else on this street already let me in."

The text says otherwise, friend. Moses tells Sihon the request is “…just as the descendants of Esau who live in Seir and the Moabites who live in Ar did for us…” So both Esau's descendants and the Moabites already let Israel pass. Moses uses that as part of his case to Sihon.

explanations.answer: He won't let them pass through
explanations.explanation: That's it. Moses says, “But Sihon king of Heshbon would not let us pass through…” Pay in silver, stay on the road, and it was still a no. I've had a baker turn down a free cookie once, and that still doesn't compare.

explanations.answer: He lets them pass right through
explanations.explanation: That would've been a short chapter, friend. The text says Sihon “…would not let us pass through…” The offer of peace gets a no.

explanations.answer: He asks for twice the silver
explanations.explanation: No haggling happens in these verses, friend. Moses says Sihon “…would not let us pass through…” and gives the reason in the same verse: the LORD “…had made his spirit stubborn and his heart obstinate…” No counteroffer is mentioned, just a refusal.

Yes, stubborn. Moses says, “…the LORD your God had made his spirit stubborn and his heart obstinate, that He might deliver him into your hand…” So Moses gives that as the reason Sihon refused. Take the words just as they stand.

Gentle isn't the word, friend. Moses says the LORD “…had made his spirit stubborn and his heart obstinate…” Israel asked to pass through on the main road and offered silver for food and water, but Sihon would not let them pass. The verse describes his spirit as stubborn, not gentle.
Weary doesn't appear in the verse, friend. Moses says the LORD “…had made his spirit stubborn and his heart obstinate…” Stubborn is the word the verse uses for Sihon's spirit.

Yes, it's True. Moses says, “And the LORD our God delivered him over to us, and we defeated him and his sons and his whole army.” Notice who he credits first: the LORD our God delivered him. The whole army and his sons are included.

It's True, friend. Moses says, “And the LORD our God delivered him over to us, and we defeated him and his sons and his whole army.” The battle at Jahaz ends with Sihon defeated. Moses gives the credit to the LORD our God.

explanations.answer: Only the livestock and the plunder
explanations.explanation: That's what Moses says: “We carried off for ourselves only the livestock and the plunder from the cities we captured.” The word "only" matters here. I think this is a heavy part of the story, friend, and Moses doesn't hurry past it.

explanations.answer: Only the weapons and the chariots
explanations.explanation: Weapons and chariots aren't named in the verse, friend. Moses says Israel carried off “…only the livestock and the plunder from the cities we captured.” That's the whole list he gives.

explanations.answer: Only the tents and the tools
explanations.explanation: Tents and tools don't appear in this verse. Moses says Israel carried off “…only the livestock and the plunder from the cities we captured.” That's the list, and he keeps it short.

Yes, walls. Moses says, “From Aroer on the rim of the Arnon Valley, along with the city in the valley, even as far as Gilead, not one city had walls too high for us.” Then he adds, “The LORD our God gave us all of them.” High walls didn't stop what the LORD had given them.
Towers aren't in this verse, friend. Moses says not one city “…had walls too high for us.” Walls are the word he uses, and he says the LORD our God gave them all.
Gates do show up in this passage, friend, but later, with Og's cities. Here the verse says not one city “…had walls too high for us.” For Sihon's cities, it's walls.

Not quite, friend. Moses says, “But you did not go near the land of the Ammonites, or the land along the banks of the Jabbok River, or the cities of the hill country, or any place that the LORD our God had forbidden.” So the Jabbok's banks were on the list of places Israel stayed away from. They didn't take them.

Right, it's False. Moses says, “But you did not go near the land of the Ammonites, or the land along the banks of the Jabbok River…” These were places the LORD our God had forbidden. Israel took what it was given and left the rest alone.

That's it. The LORD says, “Do not fear him, for I have delivered him into your hand…” Og, king of Bashan, is coming with his whole army, and the first thing the LORD speaks is "Do not fear…" That is a good first thing to hear, friend, even when the news is loud.

explanations.answer: Turn back the way you came
explanations.explanation: The LORD doesn't say that, friend. He says, “Do not fear him, for I have delivered him into your hand…” Nothing in His words sends Israel back down the road. They keep going.
No detour here. The LORD says, “Do not fear him, for I have delivered him into your hand…” He says nothing about going around Bashan. That's different from the lands Israel was told to leave alone.

Yes, land. The LORD says, “…I have delivered him into your hand, along with all his people and his land.” The people and the land both come with the king. It's the same word He used about Sihon earlier.
Gold isn't mentioned in this verse, friend. The LORD says He has delivered Og into Moses' hand, “…along with all his people and his land.” Land is the word that fits the blank.
Chariots don't appear in these verses. The LORD says, “…along with all his people and his land.” The word for the blank is land.
That's it. Moses says, “At that time we captured all sixty of his cities.” Sixty cities in the region of Argob, the kingdom of Og in Bashan. That's a lot of doors, friend, and Moses counts every one.
Close, but the number is higher. Moses says Israel captured “…all sixty of his cities.” Forty is short by twenty.
Twelve is far under, friend. Moses says, “At that time we captured all sixty of his cities.” Sixty is the number in the verse.

The text says the opposite, friend. Moses says, “There was not a single city we failed to take…” Those cities had high walls and gates and bars, and still every one was taken. He says the LORD our God delivered Og and his whole army into their hands.
Right, it's False. Moses says, “There was not a single city we failed to take…” Walls, gates and bars didn't change that. Not one was left out.

Yes, Mount Hermon. Moses says, “At that time we took from the two kings of the Amorites the land across the Jordan, from the Arnon Valley as far as Mount Hermon…” The two kings are Sihon and Og. That's the whole stretch of land Moses is summing up.
Mount Carmel isn't named in this passage, friend. Moses says the land runs “…from the Arnon Valley as far as Mount Hermon…” Hermon is the mountain at the far end.
Mount Sinai isn't in this sum-up, friend. Moses says the land runs “…from the Arnon Valley as far as Mount Hermon…” That's where the stretch ends.

That's right. The text says, “His bed of iron, nine cubits long and four cubits wide, is still in Rabbah of the Ammonites.” It also says Og was the only one left of the remnant of the Rephaim. Nine cubits long and four wide, and made of iron. I slept on a pile of takeout menus in a junk drawer, so that's a big step up from my bed.
Bronze isn't what the text says, friend. It says, “His bed of iron, nine cubits long and four cubits wide…” Iron is the word in the verse.
Cedar isn't in the text, friend. The verse says, “His bed of iron, nine cubits long and four cubits wide…” It's iron, and it's still in Rabbah of the Ammonites.
